html:
Representing confidence and uncertainty is a key goal for biological world models; comes quite naturally and is an instance of meta-learning

Metacognitive representations gate learning rates, direct information seeking and attention, and arbitrate between model-based and model-free control

Confidence representations serve multiple timescales of behavioral control, from momentary economic decisions to longer-term learning and adaptation. A 2025 study measures confidence in a hierarchical decision task (Figure) 7.

Confidence builds as trajectories approach stable attractor states, with high-confidence trials showing faster convergence to stable manifold regions.

The brain distinguishes between confidence and certainty, even though both relate to probability. One proposal defines confidence as the estimated probability that a specific decision or belief is correct, whereas certainty refers to encoding the full probability distribution of a variable (the overall predictability of the situation). This distinction implies different neural representations: confidence is a single-value assessment about a choice, while certainty involves representing spread or variance of possible states.

Probabilistic population codes and metacognitive hubs

Neural circuits appear to represent uncertainty by coding probability distributions across populations of neurons. In Bayesian brain models, each neuron’s activity can represent a "vote" for a certain stimulus value, and the overall pattern (tuning curve spread, firing variability) reflects uncertainty. For example, when sensory information is unreliable, population responses become broader or more variable, signaling low certainty about what was sensed. Conversely, sharply peaked activity patterns indicate high certainty. The brain can decode these population patterns to estimate confidence or uncertainty about stimuli. A 2025 human imaging study tests probability and confidence estimates (Figure) 5. The study maps fMRI signals associated with confidence (Figure).

An alternative proposal is that the brain may not explicitly construct full distributions at all times, but instead samples possible interpretations in parallel. In one neural model, many semi-independent modules each integrate evidence noisily; if their conclusions agree (low dispersion), confidence is high, whereas disagreement (high dispersion) signals uncertainty. In this view, confidence emerges from consensus across redundant neural processes. This sampling-by-ensemble mechanism can explain why confidence usually correlates with stimulus clarity and decision speed

Generative-model decoding of human visual cortex shows that each trial’s voxel-pattern contains a full likelihood function over stimulus orientation; the decoded width predicts subjects’ expressed confidence, directly tying distributional spread to subjective certainty 1, 2 A human experiment tests probabilistic inference (Figure) 6.

Similar reconstructions during working-memory delays reveal that parietal and occipital ensembles maintain both content and precision of remembered items 3. These findings generalize the probabilistic-population-code (PPC) idea: the intrinsic noise in a population’s firing simultaneously encodes what is represented (the mean) and how sure the system is (the variance).

Metacognitive hubs

There are dedicated metacognitive neural substrates; it is not all bottom-up

Two canonical criteria for metacognition: ongoing monitoring of internal processing and strategic control based on that monitoring

Pulvinar

The pulvinar nucleus of the thalamus stands out as a key metacognitive hub. Because the pulvinar is the only thalamic nucleus that receives reciprocal, topographically organised projections from virtually every tier of the visual and fronto-parietal hierarchy and can rhythmically gate their interactions, it is uniquely placed to fuse the many local "proto-confidence" traces that exist in cortex (e.g. evidence strength in V1, choice-related drift in LIP, value precision in vmPFC) into a single global variable. Electrophysiology, inactivation, and network-level recording all show that the pulvinar then pushes this summary out to the very circuits that set learning rates, attentional gain, and opt-out behaviour-ultimately resulting in rhythmic control of inter-areal communication and biasing downstream computations in proportion to certainty

Sensory reliability: estimate of how informative a given sensory stream is about some latent variable of interest (e.g. object location, motion direction, body position, internal states like pain or hunger). More formally, it reflects the inverse of uncertainty or variance in the mapping between sensory input and the hidden state it’s trying to infer

By collapsing heterogeneous uncertainty cues into one thalamic firing-rate variable, the pulvinar lets disparate cortical regions compare their epistemic states on the same scale-crucial for deciding whether to exploit, explore, or delegate a choice

These same neurons that encode confidence participate in large-scale alpha/low-beta synchrony that determines which cortical areas can exchange information at a given moment

Opt-out and neglect phenomena after inactivation show the pulvinar can abort actions when integrated certainty falls below threshold-something that neither LIP nor rlPFC can accomplish on their own

Because layer-5 driver axons hit granular cortical layers, confidence-weighted prediction-error information can update sensory cortices before slower neuromodulatory systems arrive, aligning plasticity with reliability in near-real time

Overall, the pulvinar decides which cortical nodes can talk to which others, at what gain, and for how long, according to the certainty of the current belief state. This mechanism turns a local, modality-bound confidence trace into a global control variable that tweaks perception, learning rate, motor gating, and conscious report-all within a few tens of milliseconds

rlPFC (right rostrolateral prefrontal cortex)

The rlPFC sits at the apex of the prefrontal gradient, receiving convergent inputs from posterior sensory, parietal, temporal-memory, and value areas and projecting to anterior cingulate and thalamic hubs; this position lets it pool already-processed "proto-confidence" traces into an explicit, domain-general certainty variable that humans can consciously interrogate or report.

Domain-general confidence code: multivariate decoding shows that a common population pattern in rlPFC predicts trial-by-trial confidence across perception, memory, and value tasks, in contrast to neighbouring mPFC which carries task-specific codes.

By integrating heterogeneous certainty cues into a single, autonoetic firing-rate/distributed-pattern signal, rlPFC enables disparate cortical and subcortical systems to compare their epistemic states on a shared scale, a prerequisite for flexible arbitration between exploitation, exploration, and memory retrieval strategies

fMRI and intracranial recordings show that rlPFC activity correlates with reported confidence even when accuracy, reaction time, and stimulus reliability are held constant, proving that it encodes metacognitive certainty rather than low-level evidence strength

Lesion and TMS evidence: focal damage to anterior/rostrolateral PFC or continuous theta-burst stimulation selectively impairs meta-d′/d′-the coupling between confidence and accuracy-without degrading first-order performance, demonstrating a causal role in metacognition

rlPFC tracks relative uncertainty in explore-exploit tasks: the higher its BOLD, the more likely participants are to sample the less-certain option, indicating a strategic control signal that adjusts behaviour when evidence is ambiguous.

Functional connectivity analyses reveal strengthened rlPFC-vmPFC and rlPFC-ACC coupling on high-confidence trials; this network appears to set learning-rate and credit-assignment parameters by forwarding precision-weighted teaching signals to dopaminergic and cingulate circuits.

Trial-resolved MEG-fMRI work places the emergence of the rlPFC confidence signal  250-350 ms after parietal evidence accumulation finishes but  200 ms before overt report, positioning it as a late but still online evaluator that can adjust decisions on the fly. 4

Overall, rlPFC transforms distributed reliability signals into a consciously accessible, broadcast-ready confidence estimate that calibrates strategy selection, learning-rate modulation, and verbal report The study examines neural correlates of posterior belief (Figure). The authors model how confidence propagates across decisions (Figure).

OFC (orbitofrontal cortex)

Sitting on the ventral prefrontal surface, OFC receives convergent inputs from multimodal sensory cortices, amygdala, hippocampus and basal ganglia and projects back to limbic, striatal and mediodorsal-thalamic hubs, positioning it to marry perceptual evidence to motivational context and predicted outcomes.

Behavior- and modality-general confidence code: single-unit recordings show that OFC neurons encode statistical decision confidence independent of the sensory modality (olfactory vs. auditory) that generated the choice and predict both trial-by-trial waiting time and cross-trial strategy updating.

By integrating heterogeneous uncertainty cues with momentary value and elapsed time, OFC converts raw reliability signals into a value-weighted, temporally extended confidence estimate that answers "how long is it worth persisting in this choice?"-a computation essential for temporal wagering, foraging and credit assignment.

Causal evidence: reversible inactivation or lesion of OFC abolishes appropriate waiting-based confidence reports while leaving primary choice accuracy intact, proving that OFC supplies a dedicated metacognitive signal rather than duplicating sensory evidence.

Human fMRI reveals that lateral OFC BOLD tracks subjective confidence after controlling for reward magnitude and reaction time, and transiently signals unexpected outcomes to primary sensory cortex-delivering top-down "teaching" signals that help re-learn stimulus-outcome mappings when confidence drops

Functional connectivity and optogenetic work show that OFC communicates confidence-weighted value signals to dorsal striatum; disrupting this loop biases economic choices without affecting sensory discrimination, underscoring a role in translating certainty into action value.

Meta-reinforcement learning: slow-timescale plasticity in OFC supports meta-RL-optimising the policy that sets learning-rate and exploration as a function of accumulated confidence; silencing CaMKII-dependent plasticity in OFC blocks this meta-learning while sparing within-session RL.

Population decoding indicates that OFC encodes both expected value and confidence in orthogonal subspaces, allowing downstream circuits to extract either variable as needed; variability in the confidence subspace predicts trial-to-trial adjustments of persistence and exploration.

Across subjects, grey-matter thickness and OFC-striatal connectivity correlate with calibrated confidence in value-based decisions, linking anatomical variation to economic metacognition

Overall, OFC transforms distributed reliability signals into a value- and time-coupled confidence estimate that governs persistence, credit assignment and meta-RL

dACC

Reads the certainty signals packaged upstream (sensory reliability from pulvinar, domain-general confidence from rlPFC, value-weighted confidence from OFC) and combines them with the current action set and motivational landscape to decide how much cognitive control and effort a particular course of action deserves. It therefore sits at the interface between abstract certainty representations and concrete motor or cognitive "affordances."

Theoretical and empirical work converge on the view that dACC computes the expected value of control (EVC): it integrates (i) the probability that ongoing behaviour will fail-closely related to low confidence or high uncertainty-and (ii) the prospective benefit of expending extra resources (time, attention, working-memory, motor vigour) to reduce that failure risk. Neural activity in dACC tracks this cost-benefit quantity across a wide range of tasks, from Stroop-like conflict to exploration-exploitation dilemmas and volatile reinforcement-learning environments The study maps confidence-related signals during decisions (Figure). The study analyzes confidence-dependent functional connectivity (Figure).

Causal evidence strengthens the bridge model: recent TMS and tDCS studies show that perturbing dmPFC shifts metacognitive bias and changes how much effort people choose to invest, without altering first-order accuracy-exactly what you would expect if dACC were reading confidence/value signals and turning them into control allocations.

Intracranial EEG and fMRI work further reveal that dACC engagement is highest when rlPFC-encoded confidence is low and the stakes encoded in OFC are high, suggesting a conjunctive "low-certainty/high-value" trigger for ramping up control.

Functionally, then, dACC closes the loop:

Monitoring. It receives certainty/uncertainty summaries from pulvinar, rlPFC and OFC, along with performance feedback and error signals.

Computation. It estimates the marginal payoff of deploying more control-effectively asking, "Given how unsure we are and how big the reward is, is extra effort worth it?"

Control broadcast. When that payoff is positive, dACC drives adjustments in dorsolateral PFC, basal ganglia and neuromodulatory nuclei, scaling working-memory maintenance, attentional focus, learning rate and action vigour

In short, dACC does not generate new confidence estimates; instead, it bridges existing certainty representations to the brain’s control and policy systems, ensuring that effort is spent only when low confidence and high stakes make it worthwhile.

The brain’s overall representation of uncertainty

A multi-tier, hierarchical certainty pipeline

Pulvinar (sensory reliability). Fast sub-cortical circuits in the pulvinar compute a moment-by-moment reliability tag for each incoming sensory stream. When that tag is low, pulvinar firing drops, monkeys "opt-out," and cortical traffic is throttled-even though raw discrimination accuracy is unaffected-making the pulvinar a global router that gates information on the basis of stimulus precision.

Right rlPFC (domain-general confidence). rlPFC reads sensory reliabilities plus higher-order and mnemonic traces to construct an explicit, task-agnostic confidence signal. This abstract code predicts subjective ratings even when difficulty and reaction time are matched, and disrupting rlPFC selectively flattens meta-d′ while sparing first-order performance. This form of confidence is explicitly inferential, informed by an agent’s internal models of the world and its own cognitive system.

OFC (value-weighted confidence). OFC binds rlPFC-style certainty to expected reward and the opportunity cost of time. Its neurons ramp with the subjective probability that continued waiting will pay off; silencing OFC leaves choice accuracy intact but abolishes the finely tuned willingness-to-wait that normally tracks confidence.

dACC / dmPFC (expected value of control). dACC receives the certainty signals packaged by rlPFC and OFC, combines them with action costs and available affordances, and computes the expected value of deploying additional cognitive control. When confidence is low but stakes are high, dACC activity rises and drives top-down adjustments in attention, learning rate, and effort allocation; perturbing dACC shifts effort investment without changing raw accuracy.

Complementary codes, complementary control

Pulvinar: low-dimensional rate and oscillatory signals deliver a rapid go/hold veto on cortico-cortical communication.

rlPFC: abstract population patterns yield a consciously accessible, domain-general confidence "common currency" that calibrates exploration, learning, and verbal report.

OFC: value- and time-weighted confidence subspace governs persistence, credit assignment, and meta-reinforcement learning.

dACC: control-demand signals translate combined certainty and value into dynamic adjustments of cognitive effort, ensuring resources are deployed only when low confidence and high stakes warrant it.

Together, these four layers let the brain compare, broadcast, and act on uncertainty at the appropriate timescale and level of abstraction-from millisecond sensory gating to strategic effort investment-turning raw sensory noise into well-calibrated, goal-directed behaviour.

Two complementary neural-coding schemes recur across areas: (i) graded rate codes where firing magnitude monotonically maps to posterior probability (LIP, OFC, pulvinar), and (ii) population probability distributions where the shape of activity across a neural ensemble encodes a full probability distribution (sensory cortex, grid cells, working memory). The brain appears to mix these codes, using graded certainty for fast action selection and full distributions when precision matters for future inference. A 2026 study investigates uncertainty during category learning (Figure) 8. The study measures task-related functional connectivity (Figure).

Detecting risk vs ambiguity

Risk describes a decision-making scenario where the probabilities of different outcomes are explicitly known. For example, choosing to bet on a lottery with a stated 50% chance of winning is a decision under risk. This corresponds to a situation of pure aleatoric uncertainty.

Ambiguity describes a scenario where the outcome probabilities are unknown or imprecisely specified. The classic example is the Ellsberg paradox, where individuals are asked to bet on drawing a colored chip from an urn with an unknown composition of red and blue chips.

Behaviorally, risk aversion and ambiguity aversion are distinct traits that are largely uncorrelated across individuals. Neurobiologically, these two forms of uncertainty recruit both distinct and overlapping neural systems.

Neurobiologically, these two forms of uncertainty recruit both distinct and overlapping neural systems. Studies comparing choices under ambiguity versus risk have found greater activation in regions such as the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC), inferior frontal gyrus (IFG), and posterior parietal cortex for ambiguous options. Other work has dissociated subjective value tracking, linking risk to the ventral striatum and superior parietal cortex, and ambiguity to the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) and superior temporal gyrus. EEG studies have also revealed distinct patterns, with ambiguity engaging a broader fronto-parietal network compared to risk. At the same time, a common valuation system involving the striatum and medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) appears to encode subjective value under both conditions, suggesting a point of convergence in the brain’s valuation circuitry.

The brain’s differential processing of risk and ambiguity provides strong evidence for its capacity to distinguish between irreducible randomness and knowable unknowns. This reframes ambiguity aversion not as an irrational bias, but as an adaptive response from a system designed to motivate the resolution of epistemic uncertainty.

Episodic memory for contextual uncertainty and asserting epistemic authority

Episodic memory allows us to assert epistemic authority; corresponds to strength of episodic trace and/or operational mode of HPC (e.g imagination mode or retrieval mode)?

Neuromodulator systems

At the whole-brain level, diffuse neuromodulator systems encode different forms of uncertainty. Acetylcholine (ACh) release is thought to signal expected uncertainty - situations where the unreliability of cues is known in advance (e.g. a noisy environment). In contrast, norepinephrine (NE) from the locus coeruleus signals unexpected uncertainty, spiking when the world suddenly violates expectations (a flash of surprise). According to this theory, ACh and NE adjust cortical gains: under high expected uncertainty, ACh biases the brain toward bottom-up information (since top-down predictions are less trusted), while NE surges act as an "alert" to rapidly revise beliefs after a surprising event. These neuromodulatory systems thus provide a global representation of uncertainty that modulates processing throughout the brain.

Even reward-processing neurons carry uncertainty information. Midbrain dopamine neurons, famous for encoding reward prediction errors, also exhibit a distinct signal for uncertainty about rewards. In one study, dopamine cells showed a sustained ramping activity when reward probability was 50% (maximal uncertainty), which was absent at 0% or 100% probability. This ramping signal covaried with reward uncertainty and suggested that dopamine not only reports expected value but also signals risk or variance. The presence of an uncertainty-related dopamine response points to a role in guiding learning and exploration - for instance, higher dopamine during uncertainty might encourage information-seeking or risk-taking behavior.
